1. More Efficient grid: No. Generating closer to use means less loss during transmission, but user-level solar is about half as efficient as larger, utility-scale solar installations. A big field of panels produces twice as much energy per square foot of panel, and transmission losses are not 50%.
2. DER: True. Distributed generation allows for a more robust grid, but solar isn't the only possibility. Combined heat and power, wind, geothermal, and smaller power plants all have this possibility. However, the grid isn't designed to handle this very well. Back when the grid was first laid out, large power plants were more efficient than small ones, so it made more sense to have large plants far away. To reverse this, we need the smart grid which requires grid investment spending, something that the author said was a bad thing in paragraph 3. In fact, rooftop solar also requires a smart grid, again - grid investment spending!

DERs, including smart thermostats, electric vehicles, energy storage, and automated appliances, can optimize consumption and supply depending on both the needs of users and the grid.

4. Peer sharing of electricity: Not really. You can already create a co-op with your neighbors, but this is a smart grid concept that is harder to implement than it sounds. You can't just run your own wires to your neighbor's house and hope it works because the energy you supply needs to have the same frequency as the grid unless you both disconnect completely. If you supply a different voltage or frequency of electricity, you can cancel out the wave to zero, or on the other hand, start fires and blow things up. Electrical appliances do not respond well to inconsistent electricity. This is why it's not quite so simple.

4. Remove public sector: Again, false. Someone has to make sure the electricity is stable and consistent, and a reliable grid is a national security concern. We can't all turn into pioneer hippies and expect our country to work as well as it needs to. Someone has to step in and coordinate things.

Luckily for you, almost everything about your credit besides overdue payments and debt collections are snapshots, and your prior history doesn't matter.

Of course, pay off old debt, especially in collections, but then:

1. Pay down credit cards - try to get the total balance below 30% of your total credit, but below 10-15% is better.
2. Consolidate any current loans if you can, since the number of open installment loans counts against you. For example, if you have multiple open student loans, it's better to consolidate to one (so long as it's not going to raise your rate).
3. Close newer credit cards. Despite the rumors stating that closing cards hurts you, it actually is good for you if you do it right. It **can** hurt you if it increases your debt utilization ratio (see #1), but if you can close a card and stay below 15% total credit utilization, it won't hurt you at all. It will **help** you because the average age of accounts is measured as part of your score. You want your average age of accounts to be as high as possible.
4. Other than those, always pay on time.

I hope that helps.

Hi! I'm an efficiency engineer, but I've spent the last 1.5 years in a procurement role. I feel your pain.

First - don't buy individual components in an attempt to build your own system. There are plenty of packaged solutions that exist; you just need to find them.

130F is considered low temperature and should be easy to produce using a variety of methods. The other consideration is how much water is needed. If it's a decent flow, then you'll need to look into a commercial-grade system. A domestic hot water heater is great in a lot of ways, but it has a small flame that can't handle a lot of usage. It's meant to pull in cold water and heat it up overnight for morning use in a home, and it won't be enough for even a modestly sized workshop unless you're only doing a couple of tasks a day.

You need commercial or industrial hot water heaters similar to this:

http://www.hubbellheaters.com/model/gx/#specs

But I'm not sure that's the right one for your needs. For one, it has a minimum flow requirement which your customer may not be able to sustain, and it is only rated for 4.6 gallons per minute with a 100 degree temperature rise. Is that enough? WHO KNOWS?

Do you or your customer know exactly what is needed? Not just the temperature, but also the flow rate, pressure needed, how to apply the water, and how to design a system to produce what is needed? You said you don't, and in my experience, the customer is an expert in their process, not in designing the support equipment that is used in their process.

So here's how I would do this the easy way:

1. Do a vendor search for companies that have products similar to the one mentioned.
2. Find their local dealers and representatives and try to figure out if they represent multiple product lines.
3. Figure out which of them have sales staffs willing to do a site visit to design a system and quote an installation.
4. Get some quotes for your customer to review, requote if necessary to refine the scope, then negotiate (or don't, it's up to you).
5. Pick the winner, customer oversees installation.

Here's how I would do this with a little more effort (if it was a high-value project, mission critical, or a large-scale operation):

1. Find multiple design-build engineering firms with hot water system experience.
2. Quote their services for all of these turn-key projects, just design, just design and installation. This is to understand their cost structure and equipment markup (see next).
3. Ask the design-build firm if they are willing to allow you to purchase the equipment directly and have them install it, according to their design.
4. Ask them for the top manufacturers of this equipment.
5. Select the design-build firm of your choice, with customer approval.
6. Solicit equipment pricing from the top manufacturers. <- should be done alongside design-build firm review as much as possible to save time.
7. Review quotes with your design-build firm as they are now your technical experts and no longer have a financial incentive to push you toward any particular equipment vendor. Ask specifics about why certain equipment/quotes are better than others.
8. Add together the equipment quote that you received to the design and install quote from the design firm. Is that total more or less than their turn-key quote?
9. If more, go turn-key route. If less, buy equipment and supply to design firm for installation.

Of course, do your purchasing thing and negotiate down the prices at each step.

You have now made sure to purchase and install the proper system, and the responsibility for getting it correct is on someone who knows what they are doing, not you or your customer. Plus, you have installed the correct system while driving down the cost through competition and negotiation, so you have provided plenty of benefit to your customer to justify your involvement.

Totally agree. OP: there's a difference between consolidating and refinancing. Consolidating turns all of your loans into a single loan, but it will have the exact same interest rate as the average of all your individual loans. You will pay the exact same amount of money as you will by doing nothing.

Refinancing your loans means that you use a different lender (sometimes the same, but not usually) to purchase your loan from whoever currently holds it. The only way they make it worth your time is to offer you a lower interest rate than what you are currently paying.

This is why the user is suggesting that you refinance a portion of your highest-interest loans.

Leave your lower-interest loans alone, and shop around for replacements for the higher interest ones. Here's my suggested strategy:

1. Go to a reputable financial advice website that lists options for refinancing student loans.
2. See what rates you qualify for at these sites. For now, you can enter an estimated amount (say 50% of your total) because you're more interested in the rate.
3. See who gives you the best rate, then fill out a formal application to refinance ALL of the loans that you have that are above that interest rate.
4. Don't worry about the loans lower than this rate; you can deal with those in a year or two when you qualify for a better rate than today.
5. Return here (or message us) if you have any questions at any point.

I just refinanced my spouse's loans through a well-known lender and have a lot of research at my fingertips still. It's a pain to do, but that's because it can save you tens of thousands of dollars over time. It's well worth the time and headache.

Yep, which is why I responded. There's a lot of information contained in the price. In fact, it's theorized that all relevant information is contained in the price:

The Underlying Assumptions of Technical Analysis
The assumption that price discounts everything essentially means the market price of a security at any given point in time accurately reflects all available information, and therefore represents the true fair value of the security. This assumption is based on the idea the market price always reflects the sum total knowledge of all market participants.

The second basic assumption underlying technical analysis, the notion that price changes are not random, leads to the belief of technical analysts that market trends, both short term and long term, can be identified, enabling market traders to profit from investing according to the existing trend.

You are trying to figure out the price based on the 'fundamentals' of the market.

There are so many chaotic variables affecting supply and demand (politics, technology, human irrationality) that I would never bet on a given outcome at any timescale.

And there is such a thing as fundamental analysis:

Fundamental analysis is a method of evaluating a security in an attempt to measure its intrinsic value, by examining related economic, financial and other qualitative and quantitative factors. Fundamental analysts study anything that can affect the security's value, including macroeconomic factors such as the overall economy and industry conditions, and microeconomic factors such as financial conditions and company management. The end goal of fundamental analysis is to produce a quantitative value that an investor can compare with a security's current price, thus indicating whether the security is undervalued or overvalued.

But that's essentially impossible. You can never know all possible fundamental factors. You cannot see inside every company and every well to know their status. Even the CEO of an energy company doesn't know everything about his competitors.

So the only way anyone can evaluate the entire market at once is to look at the price. It is the aggregate of all actors, with all of their combined knowledge about the subject. The price contains all relevant information - including the uncertainty surrounding the fact that no single entity knows everything.

So you can collect all of the data you want, but the price will tell you the net effect instantly. And it will update in real time.

The field is growing at all levels. In engineering, you can look into programs like the Department of Energy's Industrial Assessment Centers. That's where I got my start. But in any engineering program, you should be able to find clubs and organizations. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers is good, and the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers is an excellent place to interface with energy efficiency and sustainability. Plus, they love young engineers and will send you to their conferences for free. I think it's the largest engineering society in the world.

There's also research, but that will vary by school and location.

For non-engineers, there are also a ton of options. You can go into energy purchasing (like my last job) or energy sales. There are many small energy companies of all types that need all the same employees as any other company. And there are tremendous energy companies with entire efficiency or renewable energy divisions.

The major energy conference for utilities, energy companies, and large energy-using customers is organized by a prominent energy institute.

You need to be employed in an energy sales or purchasing job, or represent one of the vendors present to attend the conference itself. But you can look up the list of companies that attend each conference and research them for ideas. You will find a little of everything there, from installing renewable generation to big data analytics software packages to increase energy efficiency. There are also companies that sell gadgets like smart thermostats.

I suggest you do the same research on the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy website.

Along with all of the industry research, it's more important to make networking connections. Figure out what entities exist on your campus that research energy policy, technology, or environmental topics. There are bound to be a few institutes, departments, professors, or clubs devoted to them. Start attending meetings and introduce yourself to people. Ask professors and grad students about what they do, see if they know of internships or research positions in these areas. That's how you get started.
